summary.value: This paper presents a novel approach to periodic crystal representation by addressing limitations in existing methods for distinguishing unique crystalline structures. The authors propose a new invariant for periodic point sets, which is designed to improve the identification of unique crystals. This invariant provides a systematic approach to eliminating near-duplicate entries in material databases.

strengths.value: The paper seems to offer a substantial contribution to evaluating novelty in crystalline materials, presenting a practical and (as far as i can tell) theoretically sound method for ensuring data quality in large-scale material databases. This seems to address an important challenge in materials science research.

weaknesses.value: The relevance to ICLR is not particularly clear, as the work does not introduce a new ML method or focus on representations of ML models in the typical sense. The authors should address the relevance for iclr or machine learning in general to improve understanding by the ml community. A less technical introduction would also benefit understanding and readability. Overall, the paper may be better suited for a more specialized audience or a theory-focused computer science conference.

questions.value:
- Consider rephrasing or omitting the last sentence of the discussion, as it seems somewhat out of place.
- The paper is dense with technical details; consider moving some to the appendix (e.g. some examples) to allow more space for intuitive explanations and discussion.
- Invest more effort in improving the illustrations, particularly graphs. Figure 6’s text is small; consider adjusting the color scheme in Figure 1 to make it clearer and remove some of the elements to make it less crowded.
- The work may be suitable for a theory-focused ml conference, as it introduces a well-justified quality metric for material datasets rather than a new ML method.
- The language at times seems overly opinionated, with phrases like “notoriously hard problem” and “avoid such embarrassment.” These could be rephrased to maintain a more objective tone.

summary.value: This paper addresses identifying near duplicate crystal, using invariants computed from point distance distributions PDD. Apparently the authors found a fast method for detecting and describing near duplicate crystals, tested on retrieval experiments with several crystal databases.

strengths.value: The development of invariants to rapidly identify near duplicate structures is interesting.

weaknesses.value:
This paper seems to use a lot of language, assumptions references only clear to those studying crystal structures, and thus it is unclear if or how it links to the broader machine learning community. For example, "points" are discussed throughout the paper, it’s only in discussion where it is mentioned these points are in 3D space. There is no mention of other work using point distance distributions PDDs, e.g. distance transforms in classic computer vision, invariants such as the scale invariant feature transform SIFT used to identify near duplicate photos on a repeating pixel lattice. 

No discussion of other invariants, e.g. 3D SIFT used to characterize and detecting near duplicates based on non-repeating structures in human brain images, which would seem to work quite well in the case of redundant crystal structures, using precisely the same KD search tree structure mentioned in this work, however appear unknown to the authors, e.g.
[a] Chauvin, Laurent, et al. "Neuroimage signature from salient keypoints is highly specific to individuals and shared by close relatives." NeuroImage 204 (2020): 116208.

questions.value: Why is there no mention of invariants from well-known work outside of work repeating crystal structures? Particularly given identical technologies used for retrieval, e.g. KD-tree search trees, using invariants derived from non-repeating structures (e.g. human body anatomy) which would appear to be a more difficult problem? If these are irrelevant, it would be good to know why.

comment.value:
>This paper addresses identifying near duplicate crystal, using invariants computed from point distance distributions PDD. Apparently the authors found a fast method for detecting and describing near duplicate crystals, tested on retrieval experiments with several crystal databases.

Thank you for the high-level summary

>Strengths: The development of invariants to rapidly identify near duplicate structures is interesting.

Thank you for understanding that artificially produced near-duplicates fuel the ongoing crisis of mistrust in materials discovery, which cannot be recognized by any cell-based descriptors but can now be provably identified by generically complete and continuous invariants PDD^h.

>This paper seems to use a lot of language, assumptions references only clear to those studying crystal structures, and thus it is unclear if or how it links to the broader machine learning community. For example, "points" are discussed throughout the paper, it’s only in discussion where it is mentioned these points are in 3D space. 

Because materials are physical objects in 3D space, they are naturally represented by points in 3D space, see the first phrase of the abstract: "Periodic point sets model all solid crystalline materials (crystals) whose atoms can be considered zero-sized points with or without atomic types."

In fact, all definitions and main results hold in any dimension, not restricted to 3D space, so Euclidean space R^n explicitly appears in Definition 1.2, Problem 1.2, Definition 3.1, Theorems 4.4 and 4.5.

>There is no mention of other work using point distance distributions PDDs, e.g. distance transforms in classic computer vision, invariants such as the scale invariant feature transform SIFT used to identify near duplicate photos on a repeating pixel lattice.

The pointwise distance distributions PDDs are referenced in lines 151, 174, 183, 533, 535, and PDDs are fully introduced in Definition 2.3. We can add any recommended references, for example to SIFT. However, all these "finite-case" invariants are hard to extend from *finite* pixel grids to *infinite* periodic lattices with any (non-orthogonal) basis as shown in Fig 1 (left). 

>No discussion of other invariants, e.g. 3D SIFT used to characterize and detecting near duplicates based on non-repeating structures in human brain images, which would seem to work quite well in the case of redundant crystal structures, using precisely the same KD search tree structure mentioned in this work, however appear unknown to the authors, e.g. [a] Chauvin, Laurent, et al. "Neuroimage signature from salient keypoints is highly specific to individuals and shared by close relatives." NeuroImage 204 (2020): 116208.

We are happy to include this reference. However, human brain is a bounded object, not an infinite periodic point set. 

>Why is there no mention of invariants from well-known work outside of work repeating crystal structures? Particularly given identical technologies used for retrieval, e.g. KD-tree search trees, using invariants derived from non-repeating structures (e.g. human body anatomy) which would appear to be a more difficult problem? If these are irrelevant, it would be good to know why.

Invariants of finite sets were reviewed in lines 110-115 and 130-139, but we can include the extra recommended references. 
 
The caption of Figure 1 (left) explained the challenge: "Left: any periodic point set can be given by many pairs (cell, motif), see Definition 1.1. Finite subsets of the same lattice within boxes or balls of the same cut-off size can be vastly different. Right: almost any perturbation of atoms can arbitrarily scale up a unit cell and break the symmetry."

Invariants of finite sets cannot be easily extended to infinite periodic sets with continuous guarantees as in Problem 1.2 (c,d), because any minimal (by volume or reduced) unit cell of a periodic set can arbitrarily scale up under almost any perturbation of points (motivated by atomic vibrations). The proposed hierarchy of higher-order PDD invariants is a  very special exception by using only (sums of) distances to neighbors (not vectors to or indices/types of neighbors) because all distances change continuously under perturbations.

You are right that, after an invariant with a distance metric is computed, the search for nearest neighbors in the space of objects (crystals, not atomic centers) can be done by many classical algorithms such as kd-trees, so feel free to recommend any helpful references for this general search.

We would be happy to answer more questions.

comment.value:
The authors are apparently unaware of alternative 3D scale-invariant technology, and deflect suggestions of comparison. 

The SIFT "scale-invariant feature transform" is specifically invariant to scalings and perturbations of the type the author mentions. Specifically, SIFT specifically addresses problems with "the same cut-off size" and "perturbation of atoms can arbitrarily scale" mentioned. 

The authors state SIFT is irrelevant because it is used to describe bounded objects, and not infinite periodic point sets, however this only strengthens the argument to mention or compare against SIFT since bounded (and highly variable) objects in real image data would seem much more difficult and practical to model than infinitely repeating regular crystal structure. 

I agree "distances to neighbors" type invariants as proposed by the authors are of some interest, particularly in describing crystal structures and symmetries. I am not an expert on crystal structures, but am aware these have been studied intensely for the better part of a century in chemistry, and that the SIFT method was specifically designed to improve upon "distances to neighbors" models in realistic data contexts computer vision. There are many references describing SIFT invariants in continuous spaces, e.g. Morse theory, heat kernels.

summary.value: The work presents a novel representation for periodic crystals that allows for efficient and effective identification of de-facto duplicates in current crystal databases. In particular the representation is Lipschitz-continuous under noise, i.e., tiny variations of crystal structures, e.g. caused by measurement noise, only yield tiny distances in representation space. The representation allows the efficient identification of duplicates or (noisy) near-duplicates in databases by pairwise comparisons in databases with in total almost two million entries, thus revealing a large number of previously unknown duplicates as well as labelling errors (same structure with different chemical composition, which is infeasible) in the databases. Last but not least, the proposed approach is able to distinguish all known counter-examples, i.e. examples indistinguishable by some previous representations.

strengths.value: The work presents novel representations for periodic crystals that allows for efficient and effective identification of (near-)duplicates in existing databases. Thus the work does not only yield highly relevant practical findings, but also prevents "adversarial attacks" via claimed-new "discoveries" of materials which are however de facto already known and were only possible by exploiting deficiencies of previously proposed representations.

weaknesses.value:
The authors proposes a procedurally constructed representation, and "machine learning" in their work is limited to pairwise distance computation. In this regard, having "machine lerning" in the title is somewhat misleading. The contribution may be well suited also to be placed in a more application-oriented publication venue (Science?). However, it is clear that a representation (albeit engineered) with the stated properties that, furthermore, allows very fast distance computation is also highly relevant for any kind of machine learning on crystal structures, as manifested by the fact that previous works the authors build upon have appeared at NeurIPS and CVPR.

Note, I revised my score from 8 to 5 after contemplating the other Reviews and discussing with CLkj; see comment further down for details

In this real-world case, accuracies such as prevision, recall, F1-score etc, should be replaced by a continuous distance metric that quantifies differences between infinitely many real structures. comment.value:
Given the other reviews and discussing with CLkj, while I maintain my assessment that  the work appears to be of great value, it does seem that ICLR is not the most spot-on publication venue after all. 

In my initial review, I had inferred from two cited closely related works published at NeurIPS and CVPR that the application topic at hand has a community within the general AI community; The two cited works are 

-- Widdowson and Kurlin, "Recognizing rigid patterns of unlabeled point clouds by complete and continuous isometry invariants with no false negatives and no false positives", CVPR 2023, and

-- Widdowson and Kurlin, "Resolving the data ambiguity for periodic crystals", NeurIPS 2022.

However, I am not an expert in the application topic and I do not know their community; Hence I am not in a position that would allow me to champion the work. Furthermore, given the other Reviews, it seems that the precedence given by the two papers listed above (which are notably also both from same two authors) might not be as strong as I thought. Consequently, I am joining the consensus that the work would be better-placed in a Journal, either for a very broad audience in Science, or very targeted in a Crystallography journal.

I am joining this consensus however not without stressing once more that the work does appear to solve a highly important real-world problem with significant practical impact on research progress in Materials Science.

comment.value:
Dear reviewers and area chair,

We hope you agree with the advice of the program chairs to "focus only on the intellectual merit", so we do not need to discuss again that the paper fits the topic of "applications to physical sciences (physics, chemistry, biology, etc.)" listed at https://www.iclr.cc/Conferences/2025/CallForPapers

In fact, the keywords "continuous machine learning" in the title are highly relevant to all machine learning because most real data are given by real-valued (not discrete) coordinates. Even if we forget about atomic structures, scans of macroscopic objects include positions of corners, salient points and other features with continuous real values, which are all noisy. Experiments on finite (often manually labeled) datasets of discretizations, e.g. pixel-based images, only approximate real ground-truth data in the infinitely continuous world.

If a machine learning algorithm was not proved to be stable under noise, its output can substantially change under a slight perturbation of input. Because all gradient-based optimization implicitly assume that target functions are smooth (differentiable at  least once), the continuity is a necessary requirement for any degree of smoothness, see a hierarchy of related concepts at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smoothness  

That is why Problem 1.2 formalizing the continuity in the Lipschitz form rigorously states the future requirements for learning continuous (stable-under-noise) representations for all machine learning on real data with continuous values and hence is highly relevant to the ICLR.

We are happy to include the recommended references on SIFT features and other descriptors of finite data, though we are still waiting for exact quotes or specific references to any past results that formally prove their Lipschitz continuity needed for detecting near-duplicates.  

We were a bit surprised by the reference " Chauvin, Laurent, et al. "Neuroimage signature from salient keypoints is highly specific to individuals and shared by close relatives." NeuroImage 204 (2020): 116208" on the topic of brain imaging, which seems a bit away from our work on periodic materials.

More generally, Figure 1 illustrated why the continuity in the periodic case is much harder than for any finite data. The key reason is the discontinuity of traditional representations based on a minimal (by volume) periodic cell (also called primitive or reduced). Any such cell can be doubled (tripled or scaled by any factor) and then almost any perturbation of a single point makes this extended cell again minimal.

This discontinuity derails all past attempts to build continuous descriptors of periodic sets by using finite subsets or bounded cells.  That is why new higher-order invariants in Definitions 3.1 and 3.4 are highly non-trivial, also justified by Theorems 4.1, 4.3, 4.4, 4.5.

The discontinuity of past invariants allowed anyone to easily disguise a known periodic structure (by a slight perturbation that significantly changes a traditional cell-based representation) and claim a "new material" without justification. Sections 5-6 demonstrated the scale of the resulting duplication in the world's largest databases of experimental materials, obtained in hours instead of years (estimated for past tools, which are all discontinuous anyway). 

Because any experimental structure can be easily perturbed without changing its physical properties, all such databases should be first cleaned by continuous invariants to avoid machine learning on skewed and unrealistic data. 

The new higher-order invariants PDD^h distinguished all (infinitely many) known counter-examples to the completeness of past invariants. The computations in Example 3,.3 and B.1 were actually done by hand, which shows how easy the new invariants can be computed.

Thank you again for focusing on the intellectual merits of the paper.

metareview.value:
The paper proposes a new representation for periodic crystals and a way to identify duplicates. This is an important problem, with applications in medicine. 

In its current form, the paper is unaccessible to the general machine learning audience, as found unanimously by all reviewers. Addressing this point will require a major revision which will require another round of reviews. 

It is claimed in the title that the framework is useful for all of continuous machine learning, however the paper purely focuses on a very specific application on crystals. To better support these claims, other machine learning applications will make the paper stronger and more accessible to a general audience. 

Due to the above reasons, I recommend to reject the paper. I encourage the authors to take the reviewers feedback into account for a revision.

additional_comments_on_reviewer_discussi.value: All reviewers initially found the paper to be interesting but hard to understand for a machine learning audience not familiar with crystals. In extensive discussions with the authors and among themselves, their opinions remained the same and reviewers came to a consensus to reject the work.
